claims.text: A predictive model with explicit representations of oxygen impurities and other defect states will predict electrical conductivity more accurately than conventional analytical approaches.
The proposed accuracy advantage will apply to bulk HfNbTaTiZr in both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Conventional analytical approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The initial bulk HfNbTaTiZr is near equilibrium and contains typical alloy disorder.
The comparative specimen contains a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity level.
The model will combine computational evaluations of oxygen-related defect clusters and local disorder with machine-learning regression.
Testing will compare nominally pure bulk HfNbTaTiZr with material containing precisely controlled 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen impurities and inherent alloy disorder produce local structural disruptions, modified electronic environments, and defect-induced localized states.
Oxygen defect clusters affect electronic conduction pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit modeling of defect states captures deviations of the real material from an ideal perfect crystal.
Accounting for local disorder and impurity effects will improve correspondence between predicted and measured conductivity over the stated temperature ranges.
The enhanced model will reduce conductivity-prediction RMSE by at least 10% relative to predictions based on a perfect-crystal assumption.
Defect-free analytical models underestimate the effects of oxygen impurities and alloy disorder.
Underestimating impurity and disorder effects causes discrepancies with measurements on specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed applicability domain is bulk, homogeneous, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content around 1 wt.%.
The model's validity may not extend to nanostructured or amorphous forms or to substantially higher impurity concentrations.
Failure to reduce RMSE by at least 10% in both temperature regimes relative to conventional analytical models will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce observed conductivity trends for material containing 1 wt.% oxygen will falsify the hypothesis.
